title: GERD: Treat the Syndrome, Investigate the Alarm Features
bottomLine: Typical heartburn/regurgitation without alarm features can often be managed empirically, but dysphagia, GI bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, weight loss, persistent vomiting or other high-risk features move the patient to diagnostic endoscopy rather than indefinite acid suppression.
recognize: Typical GERD causes heartburn and regurgitation, often postprandial or positional.
Extra-esophageal symptoms such as cough or hoarseness are nonspecific and should not be attributed to GERD automatically.
differentiate: ACS, peptic ulcer disease, eosinophilic esophagitis, motility disorders and malignancy can mimic GERD.
Progressive dysphagia is an alarm symptom, not uncomplicated reflux.
assessment: Assess symptom pattern, dysphagia/odynophagia, bleeding/anemia, weight change, vomiting, medication triggers, pregnancy, NSAIDs, alcohol and tobacco exposure.
workup: Endoscopy is indicated when alarm features, refractory symptoms or another structural diagnosis is suspected; pH testing is used selectively when diagnosis remains uncertain.
Avoid repeated imaging/labs that do not answer the reflux differential.
management: Use lifestyle measures matched to individual triggers and a time-limited acid-suppression strategy when indicated.
Step down to the lowest effective regimen when symptoms are controlled and there is no ongoing high-risk indication.
Refer refractory or complicated disease for endoscopic/specialty evaluation.
medicationSafety: Review long-term PPI indication periodically rather than continuing indefinitely by default.
Pregnancy, renal disease, osteoporosis risk and interacting drugs can influence medication choice but are not automatic reasons to withhold indicated therapy.
redFlags: Chest pain concerning for cardiac disease
counselling: Teach meal/position strategies only when they fit the patient’s triggers and avoid blame-based diet lists.
Explain when persistent or changing symptoms require endoscopic evaluation.
followUp: Reassess response after an adequate trial and confirm whether ongoing maintenance is actually required.
examTrap: Refilling a PPI indefinitely for progressive dysphagia without endoscopic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Typical reflux can be treated empirically; alarm reflux must be explained.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology upper-GI guideline resources
Choosing Wisely Canada gastroenterology principles

title: Peptic Ulcer Disease and H. pylori: Diagnose the Cause and Prove Eradication
bottomLine: Peptic ulcer disease is commonly related to H. pylori or NSAID exposure. Test and treat H. pylori appropriately, stop or mitigate ulcerogenic drugs when possible, and confirm eradication with a validated post-treatment test rather than symptom improvement alone.
recognize: Epigastric pain, nausea, occult/overt bleeding and iron deficiency can occur; perforation may present with sudden severe pain/peritonitis.
NSAIDs, antiplatelets and H. pylori can coexist and multiply bleeding risk.
differentiate: Functional dyspepsia, GERD, biliary disease, pancreatitis and gastric malignancy can mimic ulcer symptoms.
A positive serology does not prove active infection after prior treatment and is not a test-of-cure.
assessment: Assess NSAID/ASA use, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, prior ulcer/bleed, H. pylori history, anemia, weight loss, vomiting and family/cancer risk.
workup: Use urea breath or stool antigen testing for active H. pylori when appropriate, accounting for medication effects on test accuracy.
Endoscopy is indicated for bleeding, alarm features, persistent/refractory disease or when direct visualization/biopsy is needed.
management: Use current eradication regimens selected for local resistance/previous macrolide exposure/allergy and confirm eradication after therapy.
Stop NSAIDs when feasible or use gastroprotection/risk mitigation when they are essential.
Treat acute bleeding/perforation through urgent endoscopic/surgical pathways.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeating clarithromycin-based therapy blindly after prior macrolide exposure or treatment failure.
Hold/adjust acid suppression before test-of-cure according to test requirements to reduce false negatives.
counselling: Explain that feeling better does not prove H. pylori cure.
Review NSAID risk and safer pain-management alternatives when feasible.
followUp: Document eradication testing and close the loop on ulcer healing/endoscopy when indicated.
examTrap: Assuming H. pylori eradication because symptoms resolved and never performing test-of-cure.
oneLinePearl: Treat the ulcer cause, then prove H. pylori is gone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology H. pylori and upper-GI resources
Canadian antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Dyspepsia: Alarm Features, H. pylori, and a Defined Trial
bottomLine: Dyspepsia is a symptom syndrome, not a diagnosis of gastritis. Look for alarm/high-risk features, use an H. pylori test-and-treat or acid-suppression strategy when appropriate, and stop cycling empiric medications when the phenotype changes or fails to respond.
recognize: Postprandial fullness, early satiety and epigastric pain/burning are common dyspeptic symptoms.
Functional dyspepsia is diagnosed after appropriate exclusion of structural disease based on risk and symptoms.
differentiate: GERD is dominated by reflux symptoms; biliary disease, ulcer, pancreatitis, cardiac ischemia and malignancy can mimic dyspepsia.
Iron-deficiency anemia, progressive symptoms, weight loss or persistent vomiting require a different pathway.
assessment: Assess age/risk context, H. pylori history, NSAIDs, anemia/bleeding, weight change, vomiting, dysphagia, family history, pregnancy and cardiobiliary symptoms.
workup: Use H. pylori testing and endoscopy selectively based on risk/alarm features and local validated pathways.
Avoid broad laboratory panels for uncomplicated stable dyspepsia without a focused question.
management: Treat confirmed H. pylori and verify eradication.
Use a defined acid-suppression trial for appropriate H. pylori-negative/treated patients and reassess rather than continuing indefinitely without benefit.
Manage functional dyspepsia with evidence-based symptom-directed therapy and reassurance after appropriate evaluation.
medicationSafety: Review NSAIDs and other ulcerogenic drugs.
Long-term acid suppression should retain a clear indication and periodic reassessment.
redFlags: Severe new symptoms in a high-risk patient
counselling: Explain that dyspepsia often has more than one possible mechanism and treatment should have a response checkpoint.
followUp: If symptoms persist or change despite an adequate initial strategy, reassess the diagnosis and need for endoscopy.
examTrap: Calling all epigastric discomfort 'gastritis' and repeatedly prescribing acid suppression without an H. pylori/alarm-feature strategy.
oneLinePearl: Dyspepsia care needs a risk screen and an endpoint for every empiric trial.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology dyspepsia/upper-GI resources

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Confirm Inflammation, Define Extent, Treat Risk
bottomLine: IBD requires objective evidence of intestinal inflammation and phenotype/extent assessment. Do not diagnose Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis from diarrhea alone, and do not treat severe flare, obstruction, abscess, toxic megacolon or major bleeding as routine outpatient symptoms.
recognize: Chronic diarrhea, blood, urgency, weight loss, abdominal pain, perianal disease and extra-intestinal manifestations can occur.
Crohn disease may be transmural/segmental and involve the small bowel/perianal region; ulcerative colitis is continuous colonic mucosal disease.
differentiate: Infectious colitis, IBS, celiac disease, ischemia and medication-related diarrhea can mimic IBD.
Elevated fecal inflammatory markers support inflammation but do not determine exact diagnosis/extent alone.
assessment: Assess stool frequency/blood, nocturnal symptoms, weight, fever, perianal disease, extra-intestinal findings, medication/NSAID use, smoking, pregnancy and infection exposure.
workup: Use CBC/CRP and stool testing including infection exclusion when appropriate; use fecal calprotectin selectively and confirm with endoscopy/biopsy plus imaging as phenotype requires.
Before immunosuppression/biologics, complete relevant infection and immunization assessment.
management: Use disease location/severity and prognostic risk to select induction and maintenance therapy with GI expertise.
Avoid chronic systemic corticosteroids as maintenance therapy.
Escalate severe colitis, obstruction, abscess/fistula complications, toxic megacolon or major bleeding urgently.
medicationSafety: Biologics/immunomodulators require infection, vaccine and drug-specific laboratory monitoring.
NSAIDs can worsen symptoms in some patients and should be reviewed.
counselling: Teach flare warning signs, vaccination/infection precautions and why steroid-free maintenance is a goal.
Address smoking cessation in Crohn disease and pregnancy planning early.
followUp: Track symptoms plus objective disease activity and treatment toxicity; ensure colorectal-cancer surveillance when disease duration/extent warrants it.
examTrap: Diagnosing IBD from chronic diarrhea without excluding infection/objectively confirming inflammation—or leaving a patient on repeated prednisone bursts as maintenance.
oneLinePearl: IBD is inflammation you can prove, phenotype, and monitor—not chronic diarrhea by label.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Crohn disease and IBD guideline library
Canadian IBD specialty practice

title: Irritable Bowel Syndrome: Make a Positive Diagnosis, Not an Endless Exclusion
bottomLine: IBS is a disorder of gut-brain interaction diagnosed positively from a compatible symptom pattern after a targeted alarm-feature screen. Avoid indiscriminate colonoscopy, imaging and food-sensitivity panels when the presentation is typical and risk is low.
recognize: Recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation and/or change in stool frequency/form supports IBS.
Subtypes are constipation-predominant, diarrhea-predominant, mixed or unclassified and guide therapy.
differentiate: IBD, celiac disease, colorectal cancer, microscopic colitis, bile-acid diarrhea, infection and medication effects require consideration when risk/alarm features fit.
IBS does not cause GI bleeding, progressive anemia or inflammatory systemic toxicity.
assessment: Assess symptom duration/pattern, nocturnal symptoms, bleeding, weight loss, anemia, family history, medications, diet, stress/mental-health factors and bowel habits.
workup: Use limited targeted testing based on subtype/risk; test for celiac disease in appropriate patients and use inflammatory markers selectively when IBD is a concern.
Routine colonoscopy is not required for every young low-risk patient with classic IBS symptoms.
management: Use subtype-directed therapy including soluble fibre, selected diet strategies, bowel-regulating agents and gut-brain therapies when indicated.
Avoid overly restrictive elimination diets without dietitian support or clear benefit.
Treat comorbid anxiety/depression when present without implying symptoms are imaginary.
medicationSafety: Review antidiarrheal/constipation agents for obstruction risk, sedating effects and overuse.
Avoid chronic opioids for IBS pain.
counselling: Use a positive diagnosis and explain the gut-brain mechanism; validate symptoms while avoiding unnecessary invasive testing.
followUp: Track the dominant symptom/function target and reconsider the diagnosis if alarm features emerge.
examTrap: Ordering repeated CT/colonoscopy/food-allergy panels for a stable classic IBS pattern with no alarm features.
oneLinePearl: IBS is diagnosed by pattern plus a targeted safety screen, not by exhausting every test.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology 2019 IBS guideline and current guideline library

title: Hepatitis B and C: Identify Active Infection, Stage Liver Risk, Link to Treatment
bottomLine: HBV and HCV testing answer different questions. Interpret HBV serologies as a pattern and confirm active HCV with RNA rather than antibody alone; then assess fibrosis/cirrhosis, coinfections, pregnancy and treatment eligibility while linking reportable infections to appropriate public-health/specialty care.
recognize: Chronic viral hepatitis is often asymptomatic until advanced disease.
HCV antibody means exposure history; detectable HCV RNA confirms current infection.
HBsAg, anti-HBc and anti-HBs patterns distinguish infection, immunity and susceptibility; HBV DNA informs viral activity/treatment decisions.
differentiate: A positive anti-HCV with negative RNA indicates no current viremia, not chronic active infection.
Resolved HBV can reactivate with significant immunosuppression and must not be ignored solely because HBsAg is negative.
assessment: Assess exposure risks, country/region history, pregnancy, alcohol, metabolic liver disease, HIV/HCV/HBV coinfection, immunosuppression plans and family history of cirrhosis/HCC.
workup: Use complete HBV serology/DNA patterns when active HBV is possible and HCV RNA to confirm current HCV.
Stage fibrosis with validated noninvasive/specialty pathways and assess liver synthetic function/ultrasound surveillance needs.
management: Link chronic HBV to current CASL treatment criteria and HCC surveillance pathways.
Treat chronic HCV with current direct-acting antivirals through an experienced Canadian pathway; most patients are treatment candidates regardless of fibrosis stage.
Vaccinate susceptible patients against hepatitis A/B as appropriate and address reinfection prevention.
medicationSafety: HBV reactivation risk must be addressed before selected immunosuppressive/oncologic therapies.
DAAs have important drug-drug interactions; review all medications before HCV therapy.
redFlags: Pregnancy with active HBV/HCV needing perinatal planning
counselling: Explain transmission, vaccination where applicable, treatment/cure distinctions and reinfection risk for HCV.
Use non-stigmatizing harm-reduction counselling.
followUp: Track treatment response/viral markers and maintain HCC surveillance for patients whose risk persists after viral control/cure.
examTrap: Diagnosing active hepatitis C from antibody positivity without HCV RNA—or assuming resolved HBV has no relevance before potent immunosuppression.
oneLinePearl: HBV is a serology-and-DNA pattern; HCV antibody screens, RNA confirms current infection.
sourceBasis: CASL 2025 chronic hepatitis B guidance
Public Health Agency of Canada hepatitis C resources updated 2025
NAC-STBBI hepatitis B guidance

title: MASLD and MASH: Identify Fibrosis Risk, Not Just Fatty Liver
bottomLine: The legacy Full-lesson slug says NAFLD, but current learner-facing terminology is MASLD/MASH. The key NP decision is fibrosis risk: confirm steatotic liver disease/metabolic context, exclude important competing causes, use validated fibrosis assessment and refer high-risk disease rather than following aminotransferases alone.
recognize: MASLD commonly coexists with obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia and hypertension and may occur with normal ALT.
Fibrosis stage predicts outcomes more strongly than the amount of steatosis or one liver-enzyme value.
differentiate: Alcohol-associated, viral, medication, autoimmune and other liver diseases can coexist and must not be excluded from one metabolic phenotype.
Normal aminotransferases do not exclude advanced fibrosis.
assessment: Assess cardiometabolic risk, alcohol, medications, viral risk, family history, weight trajectory, sleep apnea and clinical signs of advanced liver disease.
workup: Use liver chemistry plus validated first-line fibrosis scores and elastography/specialist testing when risk is elevated.
Do not order repeated ultrasound/ALT alone as a fibrosis strategy.
management: Treat cardiometabolic disease aggressively and use sustainable nutrition/activity/weight-management strategies without stigma.
Refer higher-risk fibrosis/cirrhosis for hepatology and HCC/portal-hypertension surveillance.
Use medication/surgical obesity or diabetes therapies when indicated for their evidence-based metabolic benefits.
medicationSafety: Do not stop indicated statins solely because MASLD is present; manage true drug-induced liver injury based on pattern/severity.
Review alcohol and hepatotoxic exposures.
redFlags: Rapidly worsening liver tests or systemic illness
counselling: Use current MASLD terminology and explain that the priority is fibrosis and cardiometabolic risk, not blame for body weight.
followUp: Track fibrosis/metabolic risk at evidence-based intervals and escalate when risk category worsens.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient because ALT is normal despite high metabolic risk and a high fibrosis score.
oneLinePearl: In MASLD, fibrosis risk matters more than the word 'fatty'.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association for the Study of the Liver steatotic liver disease resources
Canadian metabolic liver practice principles

title: Cirrhosis Complications: Decompensation Changes the Disposition
bottomLine: Cirrhosis becomes decompensated with ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy or jaundice/liver failure features. New decompensation requires precipitant assessment, complication-specific treatment and transplant/hepatology consideration rather than routine outpatient adjustment alone.
recognize: Ascites, edema, encephalopathy, GI bleeding, jaundice, sarcopenia, thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction are major complications.
Infection can present subtly and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis must be considered with new/worsening ascites or systemic illness.
differentiate: A high INR in cirrhosis does not predict procedural bleeding risk the same way warfarin INR does.
Ammonia level does not diagnose or stage hepatic encephalopathy.
assessment: Assess mental status, bleeding, infection, ascites/edema, renal function, sodium, alcohol/medications, recent diuresis, nutrition and goals of care.
workup: Diagnostic paracentesis is indicated for new significant ascites and many hospitalized/worsening cirrhosis presentations to exclude SBP.
Use CBC, renal/electrolytes, bilirubin/INR/albumin and cause/complication-directed imaging/endoscopy.
management: Treat the specific complication: variceal bleeding, ascites/SBP, HE, hepatorenal physiology or infection through validated pathways.
Avoid routine correction of INR/platelets before low-risk procedures when current guidance does not support it.
Refer decompensated disease for hepatology/transplant assessment when appropriate.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs can worsen renal perfusion/bleeding and are generally avoided in decompensated cirrhosis.
Sedatives/opioids can worsen HE and falls; diuretics can precipitate renal/electrolyte problems if overused.
counselling: Teach early signs of HE, infection, bleeding and fluid decompensation; review sodium/alcohol/medication safety without overly restrictive nutrition advice.
followUp: Maintain HCC and variceal surveillance, vaccination, nutrition and transplant/hepatology follow-up as indicated.
examTrap: Transfusing FFP simply to normalize INR before routine paracentesis in stable cirrhosis—or diagnosing HE from ammonia alone.
oneLinePearl: New decompensation is a complication search, not just 'worse cirrhosis'.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Hepatology recommendations updated 2024
Canadian Association for the Study of the Liver practice resources

title: Acute Pancreatitis: Diagnose Correctly, Hydrate Thoughtfully, Find the Cause
bottomLine: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed from compatible pain plus pancreatic enzyme elevation and/or characteristic imaging; not every lipase elevation is pancreatitis. Assess severity and cause early, use goal-directed supportive care, and intervene on biliary obstruction/cholangitis or other complications when indicated.
recognize: Typical pain is acute persistent epigastric pain often radiating to the back with nausea/vomiting.
Gallstones and alcohol are common causes; hypertriglyceridemia, medications, ERCP and other causes must be considered.
differentiate: Lipase can rise in renal failure, bowel disease and other conditions; diagnose the syndrome, not the laboratory number.
Cholangitis/ongoing biliary obstruction changes urgency and may require ERCP.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, oxygenation, urine output, volume status, fever, jaundice, alcohol history, medications, triglyceride risk and pregnancy.
workup: Use lipase with liver chemistry, CBC/renal/electrolytes and ultrasound for gallstones when indicated.
CT is not required immediately in every uncomplicated case; use imaging for diagnostic uncertainty or complications/severity when appropriate.
management: Provide adequate analgesia, early appropriate fluids with repeated reassessment and early enteral/oral nutrition as tolerated.
Do not use prophylactic antibiotics for uncomplicated sterile pancreatitis.
Urgently address cholangitis/obstruction and severe organ dysfunction.
medicationSafety: Avoid unmonitored aggressive fixed-volume fluid resuscitation in heart/renal disease; reassess perfusion and overload.
Review pancreatitis-associated medications and alcohol without prematurely assigning causality.
redFlags: Persistent AKI or severe electrolyte disturbance
counselling: Discuss cause-specific prevention such as gallstone management, alcohol treatment or triglyceride control.
followUp: Ensure definitive gallstone/alcohol/metabolic cause management and reassess complications after discharge.
examTrap: Ordering serial lipase to decide clinical recovery or giving prophylactic antibiotics for uncomplicated pancreatitis.
oneLinePearl: Pancreatitis is a clinical syndrome; lipase supports the diagnosis but does not manage the patient.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology pancreatitis practice resources
Canadian acute-care GI practice principles

title: Gallbladder Disease: Biliary Colic, Cholecystitis, or Cholangitis?
bottomLine: RUQ/epigastric biliary pain must be classified: transient obstruction/biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis or cholangitis have different urgency and treatment. Fever, jaundice, sepsis or persistent inflammatory findings require more than outpatient analgesia.
recognize: Biliary colic is episodic postprandial pain without systemic inflammation; cholecystitis produces persistent pain/tenderness/inflammation.
Cholangitis combines biliary obstruction with infection and can rapidly cause sepsis.
differentiate: Pancreatitis, peptic ulcer, hepatitis, right-lower-lung disease and ACS can mimic biliary pain.
Isolated gallstones on ultrasound do not prove they caused atypical chronic abdominal symptoms.
assessment: Assess pain duration, fever, jaundice, vomiting, pregnancy, hemodynamics and prior gallstone/pancreatitis history.
workup: Use RUQ ultrasound plus CBC/liver chemistry/lipase as indicated.
MRCP/EUS/ERCP are selected based on suspected common-duct stone/obstruction probability; ERCP is therapeutic and not a routine diagnostic test for simple biliary colic.
management: Cholecystitis generally requires surgical assessment and antibiotic therapy when infection/inflammation is present.
Cholangitis/obstructed infected system requires urgent antibiotics, resuscitation and biliary decompression.
Uncomplicated symptomatic gallstones require elective surgical planning.
medicationSafety: Adjust analgesics/antibiotics for renal/hepatic function and pregnancy.
Avoid delaying source control in cholangitis by repeatedly broadening antibiotics alone.
counselling: Explain return precautions and why recurrent biliary colic often needs definitive surgical assessment rather than repeated ED analgesia.
followUp: Ensure surgical/GI follow-up and confirm resolution of duct obstruction/complications.
examTrap: Treating cholangitis with antibiotics alone while delaying biliary decompression.
oneLinePearl: Biliary pain plus infection or obstruction becomes a source-control problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian hepatobiliary/surgical practice standards
Canadian Association of Gastroenterology hepatobiliary resources

title: Colorectal Cancer Screening: Screening Is Not Symptom Evaluation
bottomLine: Average-risk colorectal screening applies to asymptomatic people through current provincial/territorial programs. Rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, change in bowel habits, weight loss or other alarm symptoms require diagnostic evaluation rather than simply ordering the routine screening test.
recognize: FIT-based organized screening is common in Canada, but eligibility/intervals vary by jurisdiction and risk.
Family history, hereditary syndromes, IBD and prior advanced polyps move patients outside average-risk pathways.
differentiate: Screening aims to detect disease before symptoms; surveillance follows prior lesions; diagnostic colonoscopy evaluates symptoms or abnormal tests.
A negative FIT does not rule out colorectal cancer in a symptomatic patient.
assessment: Clarify symptoms first, then age, family/genetic risk, prior polyps/cancer, IBD, previous screening quality and ability to complete follow-up.
workup: Use the current local organized screening pathway for asymptomatic average-risk patients.
Abnormal FIT or high-risk/symptomatic presentations require diagnostic colonoscopy or specialty pathway rather than repeated stool testing.
management: Offer evidence-based screening with shared decision-making and ensure abnormal screens reach definitive diagnostic resolution.
Use pathology/history to set post-polypectomy surveillance rather than applying screening intervals.
medicationSafety: Periprocedural antithrombotic plans depend on the expected endoscopic intervention and thrombosis risk.
counselling: Explain FIT false negatives/positives and the requirement for colonoscopy after an abnormal result.
Address access barriers to bowel preparation, transport and follow-up.
followUp: Track abnormal screening results until colonoscopy/pathology is complete and record the next recall/surveillance interval.
examTrap: Ordering routine FIT for a patient with new rectal bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia instead of diagnostic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms = screening; symptoms or abnormal screening = diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology colorectal screening guidance
Provincial/territorial colorectal screening programs

title: Chronic Diarrhea: Categorize the Mechanism Before Ordering Everything
bottomLine: Chronic diarrhea is evaluated by duration, stool phenotype, medication/exposure risk and alarm features. Separate inflammatory, watery/osmotic/secretory, fatty/malabsorptive and functional patterns before ordering an indiscriminate laboratory/endoscopy panel.
recognize: Nocturnal diarrhea, blood, weight loss, anemia, fever or high inflammatory markers raise organic disease concern.
Medication effects, bile-acid diarrhea, celiac disease, microscopic colitis, IBD, chronic infection and IBS-D are common differentials.
differentiate: Functional diarrhea/IBS-D should not produce overt bleeding, progressive anemia or systemic toxicity.
C. difficile testing requires a compatible diarrheal syndrome and risk context, not formed stool.
assessment: Assess stool frequency/consistency, nocturnal symptoms, blood, weight, travel/water exposure, medications, surgery, diet, immune status and family IBD/celiac/cancer history.
workup: Use targeted CBC/chemistry/celiac testing, inflammatory markers/fecal calprotectin and stool testing based on phenotype/risk.
Colonoscopy with biopsies is indicated for alarm features or suspected IBD/microscopic colitis; normal mucosa does not exclude microscopic colitis without biopsy.
management: Treat the identified cause and correct dehydration/nutritional deficits.
Avoid repeated empiric antibiotics/antidiarrheals when inflammatory/infectious disease has not been excluded.
Refer persistent unexplained, malabsorptive or inflammatory disease.
medicationSafety: Avoid loperamide in severe inflammatory/bloody diarrhea or toxic megacolon concern.
Review metformin, magnesium, laxatives, antibiotics, PPIs and other medication causes.
counselling: Teach hydration and targeted diet changes only after the likely mechanism is identified; avoid broad restrictive diets without support.
followUp: Close the loop on stool studies/endoscopy and reassess the diagnosis if targeted treatment fails.
examTrap: Calling chronic diarrhea IBS before checking alarm features, celiac/IBD clues and medication causes.
oneLinePearl: Classify chronic diarrhea by mechanism and alarms before building the test list.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology bile-acid diarrhea/IBS/IBD guideline resources
Canadian GI practice principles

title: GI Bleeding: Resuscitate, Localize, Risk-Stratify
bottomLine: GI bleeding is managed by hemodynamic severity first, localization second. A normal initial hemoglobin does not exclude major acute blood loss; stabilize, review antithrombotics, identify upper vs lower clues and move unstable/high-risk patients to urgent endoscopic/interventional care.
recognize: Hematemesis/melena generally suggest upper GI bleeding; hematochezia can be lower GI bleeding or a brisk upper source.
Tachycardia, hypotension, syncope, rising lactate or altered mental status signal significant blood loss even before hemoglobin falls.
differentiate: Iron-deficiency occult bleeding is different from acute exsanguinating hemorrhage but still requires source evaluation.
Cirrhotic/portal-hypertension bleeding requires a variceal pathway distinct from routine nonvariceal ulcer bleeding.
assessment: Assess airway, perfusion, orthostatic/serial vitals, bleeding amount/timing, liver disease, NSAIDs, anticoagulants/antiplatelets and comorbid cardiac disease.
workup: Use CBC, type/crossmatch, renal/electrolytes, liver/coagulation studies and cause-directed endoscopy/imaging.
Risk scores can support disposition but do not replace unstable-patient judgment.
management: Resuscitate with IV access/fluids/blood products according to physiology and current restrictive-transfusion guidance.
Use urgent endoscopy/interventional/surgical pathways for ongoing/high-risk bleeding and disease-specific therapy for variceal versus nonvariceal bleeding.
Resume antithrombotics through a thrombotic-vs-bleeding risk plan rather than indefinite discontinuation.
medicationSafety: Do not reverse every antithrombotic automatically; reversal is drug-, bleed- and thrombosis-risk specific.
Avoid NSAIDs and review ulcerogenic drugs after the event.
counselling: After stabilization explain medication changes, recurrence signs and why definitive source evaluation matters.
followUp: Ensure pathology/H. pylori/antithrombotic resumption and repeat endoscopy plans are closed-loop.
examTrap: Reassuring a hypotensive patient because the initial hemoglobin is normal after acute bleeding.
oneLinePearl: In acute GI bleeding, physiology falls before hemoglobin may fall.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology 2025/2019 upper-GI bleeding guidelines
CAG/ACG antithrombotic management during GI bleeding guideline

title: Abdominal Pain: Disposition Before Diagnostic Perfection
bottomLine: Acute abdominal pain is a safety/disposition problem before it is a final-diagnosis problem. Identify shock, peritonitis, pregnancy emergencies, ischemia, obstruction, perforation, bleeding and vascular catastrophes before treating a presumed benign cause.
recognize: Pain out of proportion, involuntary guarding/rigidity, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding, syncope or toxic appearance are concerning.
Older/immunocompromised patients may have muted fever/tenderness despite serious disease.
differentiate: Cardiac, pulmonary, metabolic, vascular, gynecologic and genitourinary disorders can all present as abdominal pain.
Symptom location helps but does not replace disease tempo and associated red flags.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, onset/migration, vomiting/stool/urine, bleeding, fever, prior surgery, medications/anticoagulants, pregnancy possibility and vascular risk.
workup: Use pregnancy testing when applicable and targeted CBC/chemistry/liver/lipase/urine/ECG/troponin or imaging based on the differential.
Choose ultrasound/CT based on the suspected pathology and patient context rather than a routine abdominal CT for everyone.
management: Provide analgesia/antiemetics while evaluating; pain treatment does not need to be withheld to preserve diagnostic accuracy.
Escalate peritonitis, ischemia, perforation, unstable ectopic pregnancy, obstructed infected systems or hemodynamic instability urgently.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs may worsen GI bleeding/renal disease; opioids require respiratory/sedation monitoring but should not be withheld when severe pain warrants them.
counselling: For safe outpatient management, give concrete return precautions for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, bleeding, syncope or inability to hydrate.
followUp: Reassess unresolved pain and close the loop on pending imaging/labs rather than labelling recurrent pain functional prematurely.
examTrap: Waiting for a perfect diagnosis before transferring a patient with peritonitis or shock.
oneLinePearl: The first abdominal-pain diagnosis is stable versus surgical/vascular/emergent.
sourceBasis: Canadian emergency and gastroenterology practice principles

title: Liver Tests in GI Disease: Injury, Cholestasis, and Synthetic Function
bottomLine: A 'liver panel' contains tests with different jobs. AST/ALT primarily reflect hepatocellular injury, ALP/bilirubin help define cholestasis/handling, and INR/albumin contribute to synthetic-function assessment; falling enzymes do not prove recovery if clinical/synthetic function worsens.
recognize: Hepatocellular and cholestatic patterns narrow the differential more than one isolated enzyme value.
Albumin changes slowly and is influenced by inflammation, nutrition and renal/GI loss; INR has nonhepatic influences and cirrhosis INR does not equal bleeding risk.
differentiate: AST is not liver-specific and can rise with muscle injury.
Normal AST/ALT do not exclude advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis.
Isolated bilirubin requires fractionation/pattern interpretation rather than automatic obstruction diagnosis.
assessment: Assess symptoms, hemodynamics, jaundice/pruritus, encephalopathy, bleeding, alcohol, medications/supplements, viral/metabolic/autoimmune risk and pregnancy.
workup: Classify the biochemical pattern before ordering cause-directed viral, metabolic, autoimmune, toxicologic or imaging workup.
Use ultrasound promptly for cholestatic/obstructive concern and synthetic markers/glucose in significant acute injury.
management: Treat the cause and severity simultaneously; urgent acute liver failure or cholangitis pathways override routine outpatient repeat testing.
Persistent mild abnormalities need structured etiologic/fibrosis assessment rather than indefinite repeat panels.
medicationSafety: Do not stop necessary medications solely for a small isolated enzyme rise without pattern/severity review.
Possible acetaminophen or other toxic injury is time-sensitive.
counselling: Explain that liver injury tests and liver function are related but not interchangeable.
followUp: Trend the abnormalities that answer the clinical question and refer progressive/advanced disease appropriately.
examTrap: Declaring acute liver injury 'improved' because AST/ALT fall while INR and mental status worsen.
oneLinePearl: Read liver tests by job: injury, bile flow, and synthetic function are different axes.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Hepatology recommendations
Canadian hepatology/liver-chemistry practice guidance
